checklist.label: Pick your targets, and only your targets
checklist.detail: Three figures in this wave. Mark each one in your battle plan (tap a figure on its drop card below) so Wed Oct 14 is execution, not deliberation.

checklist.label: Set your ceiling at MSRP: $27.99 a figure, $83.97 for all three
checklist.detail: That is the announced price for this wave. Anything above it at 1 PM is a markup wearing a retail costume, walk to the next retailer instead of paying it.

checklist.label: Sign in everywhere before drop day, not at 12:59 PM ET on Oct 14
checklist.detail: Hasbro Pulse and Amazon, payment method and shipping address saved on both. A checkout queue is no place to be typing a card number.

checklist.label: Line up the backup doors
checklist.detail: BigBadToyStore and Entertainment Earth are also carrying the wave (named in Oct 12 coverage). Open their search pages before drop day so Oct 14 is one click, not a search.

checklist.label: Set the alarm for 12:45 PM ET on Wed Oct 14
checklist.detail: Fifteen minutes early is the whole game. Every 2026 window in this sequence has opened at 1 PM ET sharp.

checklist.label: Tabs open by 12:50 PM ET on Wed Oct 14, in attack order
checklist.detail: Lord Doom first, a Doom in a movie wave, and Wave 1's Doom sold out at retailers within hours of the August launch. Then Nightcrawler, then Beast.

checklist.label: Know the Pulse-lag rule before you need it
checklist.detail: On the Oct 6 Mini Comics launch, the Pulse listing trailed other retailers (single source). If Pulse shows nothing at 1 PM, that is a lag, not a sellout, check Amazon before you panic.

checklist.label: Read the price before you confirm, once, carefully
checklist.detail: The listing should say $27.99. If it says more, you are looking at a marketplace seller, not the wave. Back out and use a backup tab. (One aggregator claims prices may rise toward $30, unconfirmed; the live listing is the only verdict. See the radar poll below.)

checklist.label: Save the confirmation screen
checklist.detail: Order number, per-figure price paid, retailer. Then log what you paid in the price tracker below, receipts like yours are how the next wave's tracker stays honest.

checklist.label: If you miss, do not chase a presale above MSRP
checklist.detail: Wave 1 taught this in public: Gambit sold at $79.99 on Sep 24 and was a $25.99 presale by Oct 9. Restocks and the Spring 2027 retail release beat the launch-week premium.

captureProtocol.intro: When the window opens at 1 PM ET on Wed Oct 14, the first live listings are the record everything else gets judged against, the spread against the announced price, whether the price-rise chatter was real, and which figure went first. This is the capture procedure: four doors, worked in a fixed order, every listing written down with the time it was actually seen. It runs on the honor system and a clock, the same as the rest of the Chronicle.

retailers.name: Hasbro Pulse
retailers.role: The manufacturer's own door, and the reference price. What Pulse posts at 1 PM is the wave's own asking price, the number the price-rise question gets settled against.

retailers.name: Amazon
retailers.role: Named alongside Pulse in the Oct 12 coverage as a launch door. If Pulse looks empty at the open, this is the first place to check, a lagging Pulse listing is a known pattern, not a sellout.

retailers.name: BigBadToyStore
retailers.role: Named in Oct 12 coverage as carrying the wave. Specialist doors sometimes post a few minutes after Pulse; a later timestamp here is normal, not a discrepancy.

retailers.name: Entertainment Earth
retailers.role: Named in Oct 12 coverage as carrying the wave. The fourth door, and the one that often still has stock when the first two flip, worth the full sweep even late in the hour.

steps.label: Stage the four doors before 1 PM
steps.detail: One tab per retailer, in capture order: Pulse, Amazon, BigBadToyStore, Entertainment Earth. Signed in, search pages loaded. The checklist above gets you ready to buy; this staging gets you ready to record.

steps.label: One clock, real timestamps
steps.detail: Every entry takes the time from your clock at the moment you see the listing, recorded to the minute in ET. A listing seen at 1:03 is a 1:03 listing. Never backfill a time from memory, and never round a sellout down to the hour, the order things happened is the story.

steps.label: Pulse first, price first, in attack order
steps.detail: At 1 PM, start at Pulse and work the figures in attack order, Lord Doom, then Nightcrawler, then Beast. For each one, write down the asking price exactly as posted and the time. If Pulse shows nothing for a figure, record it as not yet listed and move on; the Pulse-lag rule says check Amazon before calling anything gone.

steps.label: Work the doors in order, one full pass
steps.detail: Amazon next, then BigBadToyStore, then Entertainment Earth, the same three figures at each door, price and time for each. Doors post at different minutes and sometimes at different prices; the spread between them is data, so do not average it away or copy one door's price onto another.

steps.label: Sellouts are events, not prices
steps.detail: When a figure flips to sold out, waitlist, or pre-order closed at a door, log the event: figure, retailer, time. No price attaches to a sellout, the last asking price it had is already in the log as a listing. A door that never listed the figure is not a sellout either; it is a door that never listed it.

steps.label: Re-sweep on the marks: 1:15, 1:30, 2:00 PM ET
steps.detail: Three more passes over the four doors in the same order. New listings and new sellouts get appended with their own timestamps. Nothing already written gets edited, if an earlier entry was wrong, the correction is a new entry that says so. The log is a record of what was seen, when.

steps.label: Close the log, then read it
steps.detail: After the 2 PM sweep, the capture closes and the post-window report below is filled from the log alone, sellouts in the order they happened, the first asking spread against the announced price, and the price-rise verdict. Anything remembered but not logged does not go in the report.

rules: Asking prices only in this log. A listing is an asking price; a completed sale belongs in the price tracker's sold lane above, never in the capture log. The two lanes do not touch here either.
No price, no listing entry. No timestamp, no entry at all. A half-remembered sighting helps nobody and quietly invents data.

Name the seller when the door is a marketplace. If a listing above the announced price is a third-party seller on a retailer's marketplace rather than the retailer itself, say so in the note, that distinction is what settles the price-rise claim honestly.
Not yet listed is a state, not a sellout. Doors post late; the log keeps the difference.
Pre-window, the log is empty, and empty is correct. Nothing goes in it before a real listing exists to record.

captureLog.note: The published capture record for the Oct 14 window. Empty until the window opens, the first entries will be the first live listings, recorded with their real timestamps as they appear. Your own capture entries, logged with the form on this page, live in your browser and feed your copy of the post-window report.

sections.title: What sold out, and when
sections.prompt: Filled from the capture log's sellout events in the order they happened: figure, retailer, time. If this section is still empty at the close of the capture, nothing sold out on the day, that is a result, not a gap in the report.

sections.title: The first asking-price spread
sections.prompt: The lowest and highest first asking price for each figure across the four doors, set against the announced $27.99 MSRP: how far the doors opened from the announced price, and which door sat at each end. Asking prices only, nothing in this section is a sale.

sections.title: The price-rise claim, settled by the listings
sections.prompt: The Oct 12 radar poll flagged one aggregator's claim that standard singles are rising toward $30, and kept the announced $27.99 because nothing else repeated it. The first Pulse listing settles it: if Pulse posts at $27.99, the claim fails on the manufacturer's own price, whatever third-party marketplace sellers ask; if Pulse posts higher, the claim stands. This section records which way the listings decided, with the listing that decided it.

sections.title: The sold lane opens later
sections.prompt: This wave ships Spring 2027, so window day produces asking prices, not solds. Any completed presale sales get logged in the price tracker's sold lane as they are reported, kept separate from the asking record as always, and Wave 1's curve says the interesting sold story is the cooling, weeks out.
